title: De Utilitate Credendi
author: Augustine

passages.original: primi generis exemplum est, ut si quisquam uerbi gratia dicat et credat Rhadamanthum apud inferos audire ac diiudicare causas mortuorum, eo quod Maronis in carmine id legerit. hic enim errat duobus modis: quod et rem non credendam credit neque id putandus est credidisse ille quem legit. alterum genus animaduerti sic potest: si quis, quia Lucretius animam ex atomis esse scribit eamque post mortem in easdem atomos solui atque interire, id uerum ac sibi credendum arbitretur. nam et hic non minus miser est, si de re tanta id quod falsum est pro certo sibi persuasit, quamquam id Lucretius, cuius libris deceptus est, opinatus sit.
passages.english: An example of the first kind is if someone, for instance, should say and believe that Rhadamanthus in the underworld hears and judges the cases of the dead, because he has read it in Maro's poem. For this man errs in two ways: both because he believes a thing that ought not to be believed, and because the man whom he read is not to be thought to have believed it. The second kind can be observed thus: if someone, because Lucretius writes that the soul is made of atoms and that after death it is dissolved into those same atoms and perishes, should judge this to be true and something he ought to believe. For this man too is no less wretched, if on so great a matter he has persuaded himself of what is false as certain, even though Lucretius, by whose books he was deceived, held that opinion.
passages.notes: Maro is Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro); the reference is to Aeneid 6.

passages.original: tertio generi est illud adcommodatum: si quis Epicurum lecto eius in libris aliquo loco, ubi continentiam laudat, in uirtute illum summum bonum posuisse adseueret et ideo non esse culpandum. huic enim quid obest error Epicuri, si summum bonum hominis uoluptatem ille corporis credit, cum iste non se dederit tam turpi noxiaeque sententiae neque ob aliam causam ei placeat Epicurus, nisi quod eum sensisse non putat, quod sentiri non oporteat? hic error non modo humanus est, sed saepe etiam homine dignissimus. quid enim? si mihi de aliquo, quem diligerem. nuntiaretur, quod sibi, cum esset barbatus, pueritiam atque infantiam ita placere multis audientibus dixerit.
passages.english: To the third kind this fits: if someone, having read a certain passage in the books of Epicurus where he praises self-restraint, should assert that he placed the highest good in virtue and therefore is not to be blamed. For what harm does the error of Epicurus do this man, if Epicurus believes bodily pleasure to be the highest good of man, when this man has not given himself over to so base and harmful an opinion, and Epicurus pleases him for no other reason than that he does not think he held what ought not to be held? This error is not only human, but often even most worthy of a human being. For what [then]? Suppose it were reported to me about someone whom I loved that, when he was a bearded man, he had said in the hearing of many that boyhood and infancy pleased him so much
passages.notes: The passage ends mid-sentence; the period after 'diligerem' in the edition is evidently a misplaced comma, and the sentence continues in the following context.

passages.original: opinari autem duas ob res turpissimum est: quod et discere non potest, qui sibi iam se scire persuasit, si modo illud disci potest,' et per se ipsa temeritas non bene adfecti animi signum est. nam etiamsi hoc ipsum, quod de Cicerone dixi, scire se quisquam arbitratur, quamquam nihil eum inpediat a discendo, quia res ipsa nulla scientia teneri potest, tamen quod non intellegit multum interesse, utrum aliquid mentis certa ratione uideatur, quod intellegere dicimus, an famae uel litteris credendum posteris utiliter commendetur, profecto errat.
passages.english: To hold opinions, however, is most shameful for two reasons: both because one who has already persuaded himself that he knows cannot learn, if indeed the thing can be learned, and because rashness in itself is a sign of a mind not well disposed. For even if someone thinks he knows this very thing which I said about Cicero, although nothing hinders him from learning, since the matter itself cannot be grasped by any knowledge, yet because he does not understand that it makes a great difference whether something is seen by the mind through sure reasoning, which we call understanding, or whether it is usefully commended to posterity to be believed through report or writings, he is certainly in error.
passages.notes: The stray apostrophe after 'potest' is a scanning artefact and has been ignored.
